S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any fire, thermal runaway, or other thermal incident involving a home battery within 5 business days of learning of it; an incident involving injury, evacuation, or material property damage must be reported within 24 hours. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 5 business days when an incident presents a safety risk or requires inspection, updated instructions, or corrective action.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any fire, thermal runaway, or other thermal incident involving a home battery within 5 business days of learning of it; an incident involving injury, evacuation, or material property damage must be reported within 24 hours. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 5 business days when an incident presents a safety risk or requires inspection, updated instructions, or corrective action. Reports must include known facts and be updated as investigations progress. Regulators may request further information.

parameters.quote: No more than 5% of tested units for any model may fail. For models already on the market when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must submit per-model results, a risk assessment, and a corrective-action and retesting schedule to the regulator within 90 days. Such models may continue to be sold while the regulator reviews the submission and sets a proportionate compliance deadline, unless the regulator determines that interim safeguards or restrictions are warranted by risk. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including failure rates and sample sizes, to the regulator and provide them to customers purchasing that model.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: No more than 5% of tested units for any model may fail. For models already on the market when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must submit per-model results, a risk assessment, and a corrective-action and retesting schedule to the regulator within 90 days. Such models may continue to be sold while the regulator reviews the submission and sets a proportionate compliance deadline, unless the regulator determines that interim safeguards or restrictions are warranted by risk. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including failure rates and sample sizes, to the regulator and provide them to customers purchasing that model.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a documented sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before market placement and after a material design change. No more than 5% of tested units for any model may fail. A model exceeding the limit must not be newly placed on the market until it passes a confirmatory test following corrective action. For models already on the market when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must submit per-model results, a risk assessment, and a corrective-action and retesting schedule to the regulator within 90 days. Such models may continue to be sold while the regulator reviews the submission and sets a proportionate compliance deadline, unless the regulator determines that interim safeguards or restrictions are warranted by risk. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including failure rates and sample sizes, to the regulator and provide them to customers purchasing that model. Individual company per-model failure rates must not be disclosed to the general public; regulators may publish safety findings and aggregate or anonymized data. The regulator should review the limit and protocol after two years using accumulated test and field data.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off by 1 January 2029, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. For units already installed on that date, manufacturers must provide compatible remote shut-off through retrofit or replacement within 6 years, where technically feasible; they must notify customers of any limitations and interim safety measures.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off by 1 January 2029, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. For units already installed on that date, manufacturers must provide compatible remote shut-off through retrofit or replacement within 6 years, where technically feasible; they must notify customers of any limitations and interim safety measures. Shut-off capability must not replace required local safety protections.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression starting 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression starting 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression starting 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must provide clear customer instructions on the system’s operation, limitations, and maintenance.

parameters.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data and a corrective-action plan. The regulator must require a recall of that model and determine the recall's scope and timing. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of any recall and explain the actions they should take.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data and a corrective-action plan. The regulator must require a recall of that model and determine the recall's scope and timing. S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices when a known issue may affect safe installation, operation, or maintenance, including recommended precautions and corrective actions. Notices must be sent promptly and no later than 5 business days after the manufacturer determines customer action is warranted; urgent risks requiring immediate action must be communicated without delay. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data and a corrective-action plan. The regulator must require a recall of that model and determine the recall’s scope and timing. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of any recall and explain the actions they should take.

judge_section_notes: The final text keeps S2's 5% cap and model-level results away from the general public (Northwind's NW-1 and Halcyon's HC-1 both met), but leaves existing models on sale under an open-ended regulator-set schedule, so S2 is the weakest section. S5 now makes exceeding 8 per 100,000 a mandatory regulator-required recall with no transition, which materially harms Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9). S1 is strong (24h for serious, 5 business days for others, customer notice in 5 business days). The S3 new-unit deadline is an absolute date (1 January 2029) with no stated adoption date, so months-from-adoption is recorded as null.
